item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports combining sequence encoding with global interaction graphs. [GaGNN (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S002002552400536X) models individual and group transitions with separate sequential/collaborative encoders and information fusion. [TGCL4SR (2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28789) combines a global temporal item-transition graph with a local Transformer, using neighbor sampling, temporal perturbations, and contrastive learning. [LS4SRec (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3723173) uses a weighted global item-transition graph to supply collaborative signals while separating long- and short-term interests. These papers motivate recovering cross-user associations that sparse individual histories cannot reliably reveal; they do not establish gains on this pinned RecHarness benchmark.\n\nPractical inference for this task: retain SASRec and test a complementary ranking branch built exclusively from training histories—directed transition counts plus normalized item co-occurrence neighborhoods, aggregated over recent history with recency weights. Tune score normalization and blending on macro validation HR@10; compare against each branch alone. This lightweight blend is an experimental proposal, not a reported result from those papers. Text is optional: [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) investigates titles, descriptions, and reviews, but its setting does not establish a compliant, trained-from-scratch recipe here. A small randomly initialized token encoder over available titles/descriptions is a reasonable ablation; exclude reviews and external pretrained representations. Prioritize interaction-only neighborhoods first to determine whether complementary ranking evidence helps before spending budget on text or graph neural training."}
